wholeQuestion.question: Which intake history is most clinically informative?
choices: Estimated proportion of usual intake, duration, and reason for reduction
The name of the last meal only
wholeQuestion.rationale: Magnitude, duration, and mechanism allow the team to interpret nutrition risk.

choiceReview.choice: Estimated proportion of usual intake, duration, and reason for reduction
choiceReview.assessment: Relative reduction, duration and cause provide interpretable intake history.

choiceReview.choice: The name of the last meal only
choiceReview.assessment: The last meal alone omits typical intake and duration.
Preferences alone do not quantify inadequate intake.
Glucose is not an intake history.

wholeQuestion.question: Which finding most directly suggests impaired assimilation?
choices: Persistent diarrhea after major intestinal resection
Stable intake with normal bowel function
wholeQuestion.rationale: Altered anatomy and persistent losses can reduce nutrient absorption.

choiceReview.choice: Persistent diarrhea after major intestinal resection
choiceReview.assessment: Intestinal resection with persistent diarrhea suggests impaired assimilation; it is not proof that every diarrhea episode is malabsorption.
Food preference can affect intake but does not directly indicate assimilation failure.
Intentional restriction concerns intake, not evidence of intestinal absorption failure.

choiceReview.choice: Stable intake with normal bowel function
choiceReview.assessment: Stable intake and normal bowel function do not most directly suggest impaired assimilation.

wholeQuestion.question: Why must weight loss be classified as intentional or unintentional?

Only intentional loss can be severe
wholeQuestion.rationale: Unintentional loss generally signals disease, inadequate intake, or impaired assimilation.

choiceReview.choice: Intent changes the clinical meaning and likely mechanism
choiceReview.assessment: GLIM uses nonvolitional loss; intentional change needs a different contextual interpretation.
Intent does not alter the percentage formula.
Intent does not determine measured height.

choiceReview.choice: Only intentional loss can be severe
choiceReview.assessment: The source does not restrict severe weight loss to intentional loss.

wholeQuestion.question: Which medication effect can plausibly reduce nutrition intake?
wholeQuestion.rationale: Medication related nausea can create or sustain inadequate intake.

choiceReview.assessment: Nausea is a supporting gastrointestinal symptom that can plausibly impair intake; a medication contribution requires review rather than an automatic causal attribution.
Improved swallowing can relieve an intake barrier.
Resolved pain can relieve an intake barrier.
Improved food access can relieve an intake barrier.

wholeQuestion.question: What is the best way to characterize disease burden in a nutrition assessment?
choices: Integrate diagnosis, inflammatory stress, symptoms, and metabolic demand
Assume every chronic disease causes identical stress
wholeQuestion.rationale: The effect of disease depends on activity, severity, inflammation, and functional consequences.

choiceReview.choice: Integrate diagnosis, inflammatory stress, symptoms, and metabolic demand
choiceReview.assessment: GLIM inflammation guidance and Academy/ASPEN clinical assessment consider disease, severity, symptoms and catabolic context.
A diagnostic name alone omits activity and severity.
Albumin alone does not characterize the complete disease and nutrition context.

choiceReview.choice: Assume every chronic disease causes identical stress
choiceReview.assessment: Chronic diseases do not necessarily produce identical inflammatory burden.

wholeQuestion.rationale: The identified barrier should drive urgent swallowing and symptom evaluation.

choiceReview.assessment: Painful swallowing is the stated barrier and calls for appropriate swallowing and symptom assessment. The stem does not establish aspiration or prescribe a feeding route.
The history does not suggest excess absorption.
The history does not state intentional weight gain.
An assay error does not explain the reported painful swallowing.

Do you prefer tablets or capsules?

choiceReview.assessment: The direct question explores whether access limited food availability; it is an original clinical question, not a newly validated screening instrument.

choiceReview.assessment: GLIM and Academy/ASPEN intake criteria explicitly combine intake magnitude and duration.
Duration does not change height.

wholeQuestion.question: Which pattern is most compatible with chronic disease related inflammation?
choices: Progressive muscle loss with active chronic inflammatory disease
One skipped meal before a procedure

choiceReview.assessment: Active chronic inflammatory disease with tissue loss is compatible with chronic inflammatory catabolism, not by itself a complete diagnosis.

choiceReview.choice: One skipped meal before a procedure
choiceReview.assessment: A skipped meal alone does not demonstrate chronic inflammation.

wholeQuestion.question: What should be done when the reported intake and observed meal consumption conflict?

choiceReview.choice: Clarify the time frame and triangulate with records and caregivers
choiceReview.assessment: The Academy/ASPEN history section uses patient/caregiver information, observed intake and records; reconcile interval and differing observations.

Discarding every observation loses potentially useful measured evidence.

wholeQuestion.question: Which weight is most appropriate for interpreting tissue change in a patient with marked edema?
choices: Measured weight interpreted with fluid status, credible prior weights, and documented uncertainty

wholeQuestion.rationale: Fluid accumulation can mask tissue loss, so volume status and uncertainty must be explicit.

choiceReview.choice: Measured weight interpreted with fluid status, credible prior weights, and documented uncertainty
choiceReview.assessment: Fluid-confounded weight needs volume context, credible history and explicit uncertainty, not automatic substitution of a precise dry-weight estimate.

choiceReview.choice: A weight selected to produce a normal BMI
choiceReview.assessment: Selecting a weight to force a normal BMI introduces arbitrary bias.

choiceReview.choice: Any historical weight regardless of date

Weights from different scales at random times

wholeLesson.title: History, Intake, and Disease Burden
wholeLesson.summary: Nutrition status is a trajectory. The history explains the direction and speed of change better than a single measurement.
wholeLesson.application: Reconstruct what changed, when it changed, and why. Separate poor access, poor appetite, impaired swallowing, malabsorption, losses, and elevated metabolic demand.

lesson.heading: Quantify the trajectory
lesson.body: Record usual weight, current measured weight, the time interval, whether the change was intentional, and whether fluid shifts could distort the result. Estimate the proportion of usual intake being consumed and the duration of the reduction.

lesson.heading: Identify the mechanism
lesson.body: Reduced intake can reflect nausea, pain, dysphagia, altered taste, depression, food insecurity, medication effects, or treatment schedules. Gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea can impair intake or assimilation. Review malabsorptive disorders, altered anatomy, and gastrointestinal losses as distinct mechanisms affecting nutrient availability. Disease burden can add inflammatory and catabolic stress.

keyPoints: Ask about duration, not only current intake.
Review medications as possible causes of anorexia, nausea, altered taste, diarrhea, or constipation.

choices: Food intake below half of estimated needs for more than one week
check.rationale: Sustained reduction in food intake can satisfy the reduced intake or assimilation etiologic criterion.

bodyReview.assessment: Baseline, current measurement, interval, intent and fluid context match clinical weight/intake histories.

Gastrointestinal symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea can impair intake or assimilation. Review malabsorptive disorders, altered anatomy, and gastrointestinal losses as distinct mechanisms affecting nutrient availability. Disease burden can add inflammatory and catabolic stress.

bodyReview.assessment: Separate intake barriers, gastrointestinal symptoms, actual malabsorptive/anatomic conditions and inflammatory stress; supporting symptoms do not automatically prove malabsorption.

wholeLesson.title: Anthropometrics and Body Composition
wholeLesson.summary: Weight and BMI are useful when their limitations are visible. Muscle and fat loss may be clinically important even when body weight appears ordinary.
wholeLesson.application: Use measured values when possible, compare them with a credible baseline, calculate percent change, and interpret the result alongside edema, ascites, obesity, amputation, and body composition.

lesson.heading: Calculate before classifying
lesson.body: Percent weight loss equals usual weight minus current weight, divided by usual weight, multiplied by 100. BMI equals weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Neither value should be interpreted without the clinical timeline and measurement conditions.

lesson.heading: Recognize hidden depletion
lesson.body: Edema and ascites can mask tissue loss. A person with a high BMI can still have low muscle mass and clinically important malnutrition. Repeated measurements obtained under similar conditions are more informative than isolated values.

keyPoints: Record measured weight and fluid status. Use credible prior weights and other assessment findings when fluid shifts obscure tissue change; label estimates and their uncertainty.
State whether height and weight were measured, reported, or estimated.
BMI does not directly measure muscle mass.
